summary: This standards-track memo extends MIME parameter value and encoded-word mechanisms to handle character sets, languages and continuations for long values. It was replaced by RFC 2231.

plainLanguage.summary: Letting long or foreign-language labels in email be split and written properly.

questions: how do mime parameter continuations work
how do you send non-ascii parameter values in email
what is the purpose of the asterisk in mime parameter names
how do you specify language in mime parameters
subtitle: Extending MIME to handle character sets, languages, and long parameter values.

tldr.problem: MIME parameter values (like filenames in attachments) are limited to 7-bit ASCII and cannot be split across header lines, creating problems for long values and non-ASCII text.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends MIME with continuation syntax using numbered parameters (like filename*0, filename*1) to split long values, and adds character set and language information using a special syntax with single quotes and percent encoding.
tldr.outcome: Email can now include attachment filenames, content descriptions, and other parameters in any language and with any length. It was later replaced by RFC 2231 with minor refinements.

facts.label: Parameter continuation syntax
facts.value: Asterisk followed by decimal index (filename*0, filename*1, ...)

facts.label: Percent encoding
facts.value: Percent sign followed by 2 hex digits (%20 for space)

today: RFC 2184 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2231. RFC 2231 provides the same mechanisms with minor refinements.

sections.title: The MIME Parameter Limitation
sections.content:
MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) is the standard for non-ASCII text and attachments in email. However, MIME parameter values like Content-Type headers have three limitations. First, email header lines must be wrapped according to RFC 822 rules, which can damage long parameter values that have no obvious break points. Second, MIME headers are limited to 7-bit ASCII, and the RFC 2047 encoded-word mechanism for non-ASCII text cannot be used in parameter values, making it impossible to have parameter values in other character sets without custom encoding.

Third, character set information alone is insufficient for proper display of some text. For example, reading text aloud requires knowing the language it is written in. Parameter values that will be displayed to users need language information.
sections.plainLanguage: Email headers can only use plain English letters. If you want to send a file with a name in Japanese, or a really long filename, email breaks things.

sections.title: Breaking Long Values Into Pieces
sections.content:
The RFC solves the line-wrapping problem by allowing a single parameter value to be split across multiple parameters with numeric indices. An asterisk followed by a decimal count is appended to the parameter name to indicate continuation. For example, a long URL can be split as: URL*0="ftp://" followed by URL*1="cs.utk.edu/...". The original value is recovered by concatenating the segments in order.

Numbering starts at 0 and increments by 1 with no gaps or leading zeros allowed. Quotes around parameter values are part of the syntax but not part of the value itself. Continuation segments can be mixed quoted and unquoted freely.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one long parameter, send several numbered parameters (title*0, title*1, title*2) and the email program glues them back together.

sections.title: Character Sets and Languages
sections.content:
To include non-ASCII characters and language information, parameter names ending in an asterisk indicate that character set and language data are present. The syntax is: charset'language'encoded-value, separated by single quotes. For example: title*=iso-8859-1'fr'Caf%E9 means the value is in ISO 8859-1, French language, and the text Café is percent-encoded.

Either the charset or language field (or both) can be left blank, but the single quote delimiters MUST be present. Octets are encoded in percent-encoded form (e.g., %20 for space, %C3%A9 for é in UTF-8), matching the syntax used in RFC 2047.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the actual text, you write what character set and language it is in, separated by quote marks. Then special characters are written as %HEX.

sections.title: Combining Continuations With Encoding
sections.content:
Character set and language information can be combined with continuation indices. For example: title*1*=iso-8859-1'en'part%20one and title*2="part two". When multiple segments are used, language and character set information appears only at the start of the first segment.

If the first segment is encoded (with character set and language), all subsequent segments are concatenated directly. An important rule is that the first segment of a continued parameter MUST be encoded if any character set or language information is provided.
sections.plainLanguage: When splitting a long foreign-language value, the charset and language tags go on the first piece only. Remaining pieces are concatenated directly.

sections.title: Language in Encoded Words
sections.content:
RFC 2047 defined encoded-words for non-ASCII text in headers. This RFC extends encoded-words to carry language information by adding an asterisk and language tag after the character set name. For example: =?US-ASCII*EN?Q?Keith_Moore?= is an encoded word in US-ASCII for English-language display.

The language tag follows RFC 1766 conventions, allowing applications like screen readers to select the appropriate voice or pronunciation for displayed text.
sections.plainLanguage: When an email header has foreign text, you can now say what language it is so the computer knows how to read it aloud.

sections.title: Server Processing
sections.content: IMAP4 servers should decode parameter value continuations when generating BODY and BODYSTRUCTURE responses. This means that when a mail client asks the server about a message's structure, the server reassembles the split parameters into their original form, so the client does not have to parse continuation syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail servers can reassemble split parameters so clients receive the full value, making it easier for email programs to handle.

data.title: Split parameter with encoding
data.code:
Content-Type: application/x-stuff
 title*1*=utf-8'en'This%20is%20
 title*2="a long value"
